input.step_by_step_reasoning: The whiteboard shows 7 components: two Kinesis streams (input event stream and output event stream), two Lambda functions (lean reader and NLP worker), two RDS databases/tables (raw transactions and extracted data) and one SQS queue. The two Kinesis, two Lambda and two RDS icons perform distinct steps, so they are kept as separate nodes (no fusion). No generic actors needed pruning. Jenkins/CloudFormation are only mentioned as deployment tooling and the upstream account aggregation service is not drawn, so neither is added. Flow 0 (ingestion/fan-out): Kinesis #1 delivers the 'account updated' event (account ID) and triggers the lean Lambda, which queries RDS for the user's transactions, receives them, batches them (~100) and publishes the description strings to SQS. Flow 1 (NLP processing): SQS fans out to many NLP Lambdas, which parse the descriptions with an ANTLR-generated parser, write the extracted fields plus model version to RDS, and publish a completion event to Kinesis #2 for other teams. Ledger edges not described in the audio (SQS -> reader Lambda, NLP Lambda -> SQS, RDS extracted -> NLP Lambda, Kinesis #2 -> NLP Lambda) are still emitted with type 'data' and empty notes. Self-check: visual_connections entries = 11; edges emitted = 11.

graph.name: Tandem: Transaction Enrichment Pipeline with NLP on Lambda
graph.categories: Serverless, Data Pipeline, Machine Learning, NLP, Financial Services
graph.notes: Tandem bank enriches aggregated bank transaction data. An account-updated event on Kinesis triggers a lean Lambda that reads the user's transactions from RDS and batches them into SQS. A fan-out tier of Lambda functions hosting an ANTLR-based NLP parser extracts merchant, location, currency, exchange rate and dates, stores the results with the model version in RDS, and publishes a completion event to a second Kinesis stream. Tens of millions of transactions; SQS was introduced because a Kinesis shard allows only one sequential Lambda consumer. Model deployed via Jenkins and CloudFormation (not drawn).

nodes.name: Kinesis #1 (account updated event stream)
nodes.notes: Receives an event containing an account ID when an upstream account aggregation service has updated a user's account (triggered by schedule or when the user logs in/refreshes the app). Only one Lambda can be attached per shard and it processes sequentially.

nodes.name: Lambda - Reads user data from RDS and puts it to SQS
nodes.notes: Purposely very lean and fast. Runs a SQL query against RDS for the user's transactions, groups them into batches of about 100 and publishes the transaction description strings to SQS.

nodes.name: RDS - Stores transactional data
nodes.notes: Holds raw transactions (date, description, amount) written by the upstream account aggregation service that collects data from third-party UK banks.

nodes.name: SQS
nodes.notes: Queue of batched raw transaction description strings. Introduced to fan out processing because the Kinesis-attached Lambda could not keep up with tens of millions of transactions.

nodes.name: Lambda - Hosts NLP model to extract required information
nodes.notes: Second Lambda tier that scales out massively. Hosts a parser generated with ANTLR from a domain-specific grammar compiled to Python, with glue logic. Processing takes a few seconds. Extracts merchant name, merchant location, currencies, exchange rates and dates. Bundled with Python dependencies and C extensions by a custom open source tool; deployed through Jenkins and CloudFormation.

nodes.name: RDS - Stores the extracted data
nodes.notes: Table with columns for all extracted fields. Stores processed transactions together with the version of the model that was run, for later analysis, comparison and model iteration.

nodes.name: Kinesis #2 (processing finished event stream)
nodes.notes: Event stream signalling that the customer's transactions have been processed; other parts of the organization trigger from it, e.g. to refresh the app with friendly descriptions.

edges.notes: Account-updated event carrying the account ID triggers the lean Lambda.
SQL query requesting the transactions for the given user.
Returns the user's raw transactions.
Publishes messages with batches of about 100 transaction description strings.
Queue messages fan out to many concurrent NLP Lambda invocations with the batched raw descriptions.
Writes the extracted/enriched transaction fields along with the model version used.
Publishes an event that the customer's transactions have finished processing, for downstream consumers.
